entry: Genus of more than 1,000 species of [[Flowering plant|flowering plants]] in the family Balsaminaceae, widely distributed throughout the [[Northern Hemisphere]] and the [[Tropics|tropics]]. Most species are herbaceous annuals or perennials with succulent stems, from five centimeters to 2.5 meters tall. The scientific name, Latin for "impatient," and the common name "touch-me-not" refer to the explosive dehiscence of the seed capsules, which scatter seeds up to several meters away. Most species grow in tropical and subtropical mountain forests of Africa, Madagascar, the Himalayas, the [[Western Ghats]] and Southeast Asia. Europe has only one native species, *Impatiens noli-tangere*. Himalayan balsam (*I. glandulifera*) is an invasive weed that displaces smaller plants along riverbanks, increasing [[Erosion|erosion]]. The genus ranks among the top three bedding plant genera, and busy lizzie (*I. walleriana*) is widely cultivated.

Procedure by which a legislative body or other tribunal initiates charges against a public official for misconduct. It is usually reserved for serious abuses of office and generally requires a supermajority. From 1990 to 2020 there were at least 272 impeachment charges against 132 heads of state in 63 countries. Most democracies involve the courts in the process, but the [[United States]] is a notable exception. Under the U.S. Constitution the House of Representatives has the sole power to impeach and the Senate the sole power to try impeachments. Impeachment differs from a no-confidence motion, which can remove a government and its ministers from office.

Reigning dynasty of Japan, made up of members of the emperor's extended family who undertake official duties. The imperial house recognizes 126 monarchs, beginning with Emperor Jimmu, traditionally dated to 660 BC but considered mythical. Verifiable emperors begin with Kinmei in 539. The current emperor, [[Naruhito]], succeeded his father, [[Akihito]], in 2019. Under the 1947 constitution the emperor is "the symbol of the State and of the unity of the people" with no role in government. The Japanese [[Monarchy|monarchy]] is the oldest continuous hereditary monarchy in the world.

System of measurement first defined in the British Weights and Measures Act 1824. It developed from earlier English units, replacing the Winchester Standards (in effect 1588 to 1825), and came into official use across the [[British Empire]] in 1826. The 1824 act gave the imperial gallon as 277.274 cubic inches (4.54371 liters); the Weights and Measures Act 1985 defined it as exactly 4.54609 liters. By the late 20th century most nations of the former empire had adopted the [[Metric system|metric system]] as their main system. Imperial units remain in use alongside metric units in the United Kingdom and in some other former imperial territories, notably Canada. The system is distinct from the related customary units of the United States.

Contagious bacterial infection of the superficial skin, usually caused by *Staphylococcus aureus* or *Streptococcus pyogenes*. Its most common form causes yellowish crusts on the face, arms or legs. It affected about 140 million people, 2% of the world population, in 2010, most often children aged two to five. Treatment is typically with antibiotic creams such as mupirocin, while [[Cefalexin|cefalexin]] is given by mouth for large areas. Without treatment most cases improve within three weeks. Complications may include cellulitis or poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis. The name is from the Latin *impetere*, "attack."

Hue that cannot be perceived under ordinary viewing conditions. [[Color theory|Opponent process theory]] holds that the visual system encodes color in three opposing channels: red versus green, blue versus yellow, and black versus white. Because the medium-wavelength cones overlap the responses of the other cones, no light can excite them alone. In April 2025 a research group reported using a retinal scanner and a steerable laser to stimulate only these cones, producing a "hyper-green" greener than any physically possible green.

19th-century art movement begun in [[Paris]] in the 1870s and 1880s, characterized by visible brushstrokes, ordinary subjects and the depiction of changing light. Impressionists painted outdoors, or en plein air, and used short, broken strokes of unmixed color to capture momentary effects of light and atmosphere rather than detail. The name derives from [[Claude Monet]]'s *Impression, Sunrise*, which the critic Louis Leroy mocked in a satirical 1874 review of the First Impressionist Exhibition. Core members included [[Pierre-Auguste Renoir]], [[Camille Pissarro]] and Edgar Degas. Academic painting standards of the Académie des Beaux-Arts had favored finished, historical and religious subjects. Impressionism prefigured [[Post-Impressionism]], Fauvism and [[Cubism]].

Theatrical form, often comedic, in which most or all of the performance is unscripted and created spontaneously by the performers. The earliest well-documented Western use of improvisation is the Atellan Farce of 391 BC. From the 16th to the 18th centuries, [[Commedia dell'arte|commedia dell'arte]] performers improvised around broad outlines in Italy. In the 1890s [[Konstantin Stanislavski]] and Jacques Copeau made improvisation central to acting training. Viola Spolin developed improvisation games in the 1940s, '50s and '60s. Many current rules of comedic improv were formalized in [[Chicago]] in the late 1950s and early 1960s, at The Compass Players and The Second City. Applied improvisation is used in classrooms, businesses and sometimes [[Psychotherapy|psychotherapy]].

[[Bomb]] constructed and deployed in ways other than conventional military action, often from homemade or scavenged parts. The term "IED" was coined by the British Army during the Northern Ireland conflict for booby traps made by the IRA and entered common use in the U.S. during the [[Iraq War]]. IEDs are used mainly by violent non-state actors such as guerrilla and terrorist groups, though state special forces also use them. They may combine military explosives, such as [[Artillery|artillery]] shells, with homemade explosives. Triggers include remote control, [[Infrared|infrared]] or magnetic sensors, pressure plates and trip wires. Antipersonnel devices often contain nails or ball bearings. Some builders use components from [[Mobile phone|mobile phones]], washing machine timers or garage door openers. Toxic chemical, biological or radioactive ("dirty bomb") material may be added.

Change in [[Momentum|momentum]] of an object, usually produced by a comparatively large force acting over a short time, as in an impact or collision. Impulse is a vector quantity with the same units as momentum. For a force acting over time, impulse is the integral of force with respect to time; for constant mass it equals the change in velocity multiplied by mass, J = Δp = mv₂ − mv₁. Its SI unit is the newton-second (N⋅s), equivalent to the kilogram-meter per second. Collisions are often idealized as instantaneous changes, a useful model in video game physics engines. In [[Rocket|rocketry]], "total impulse" is synonymous with impulse, and specific impulse, the impulse per unit mass of propellant, relates a vehicle's change in velocity through the Tsiolkovsky rocket equation.

Pakistani former cricketer and politician, prime minister of Pakistan from 2018 to 2022. He captained Pakistan to victory at the 1992 [[Cricket World Cup]]. He led the Pakistan Tehreek-e-Insaf (PTI) party from 1996 to 2023. In the 2018 general election he won all five constituencies he contested. He was the first Pakistani prime minister removed by a no-confidence motion, in April 2022. Sentenced to prison in January 2025 and again in December, he has been held in Adiala Jail in [[Rawalpindi]] since 2023. He says his imprisonment is politically motivated, a claim denied by the Shehbaz Sharif government and the post-2022 military establishment.

Hungarian communist politician, prime minister in 1953–55 and leader of the [[Hungarian Revolution of 1956]]. He tried to relax the Stalinist policies of Mátyás Rákosi but was forced out in 1955. Reinstated as prime minister on October 24, 1956, he withdrew Hungary from the [[Warsaw Pact]] on November 1. Soviet forces invaded on November 4 and deposed him; he took refuge in the Yugoslav embassy until he was lured out on November 22 and deported to Romania. He was tried for treason, executed and buried in an unmarked grave. He was rehabilitated and reburied with full honors in June 1989.

War poem in the form of a rondeau, written during [[World War I]] by Canadian physician John McCrae. McCrae wrote it on May 3, 1915, after presiding over the funeral of his friend Lieutenant Alexis Helmer, who died in the Second Battle of Ypres. It was first published on December 8, 1915, in the London magazine Punch. Its red poppies growing over soldiers' graves made the remembrance poppy one of the world's most recognized memorial symbols. The poem is a prominent [[Remembrance Day]] symbol across the [[Commonwealth of Nations]], especially in Canada.

Seven-volume novel by French author [[Marcel Proust]], published in France between 1913 and 1927. Known for its length and its theme of involuntary memory, it was translated into English as *Remembrance of Things Past*. The narrator recalls his childhood and adult life in late 19th- and early 20th-century high society. Proust worked on the novel from 1909 until his final illness in 1922. The last three of the seven volumes existed only in draft form, and his brother Robert oversaw their publication. The second volume won the 1919 Prix Goncourt. The novel influenced 20th-century literature, and it holds the Guinness World Record for longest novel.

2000 romantic drama film by [[Wong Kar-wai]], set in 1962 [[British Hong Kong|British Hong Kong]]. Tony Leung and Maggie Cheung play neighbors who suspect their spouses of an affair. It is the second film in an informal trilogy, after *Days of Being Wild* (1990) and before *2046* (2004). Leung won the Best Actor award at the 53rd [[Cannes Film Festival]], becoming the first Hong Kong actor to receive it. The film was Hong Kong's submission for Best International Feature Film at the 73rd Academy Awards but was not nominated. It is often listed among the greatest films of all time.

Assisted reproductive technology in which an egg is fertilized with sperm in a laboratory, and the resulting embryo is transferred to the [[Uterus|uterus]]. It is used to treat [[Infertility|infertility]], enable [[Surrogacy|gestational surrogacy]] and avoid some inherited genetic conditions. The Latin term *in vitro* means "in glass." In July 1978 Louise Brown became the first child born after IVF, at a hospital in Royton, Oldham, England. Robert Edwards, a member of the development team, received the 2010 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. In 2023 an estimated twelve million children had been born worldwide using IVF and other assisted reproduction techniques.

Ancient [[Mesopotamia|Mesopotamian]] goddess of war, love and sex, also associated with political power and divine law. Originally worshipped in [[Sumer]], she was known to the Akkadians, Babylonians and Assyrians as Ishtar. Her primary title was "Queen of Heaven," and she was patron goddess of the Eanna temple at [[Uruk]]. She was worshipped in three forms, two of which reflect the phases of the planet [[Venus]]. Her symbols include the lion and the eight-pointed star. In her most famous myth she descends to the underworld, ruled by her sister Ereshkigal, is struck dead there and is rescued after Enki sends two beings. Her husband Dumuzid is taken in her place, and the cycle of the seasons results from his and his sister's alternating time in the underworld.

Production of offspring from closely related organisms. Inbreeding increases homozygosity, which can expose harmful recessive traits and cause inbreeding depression, a temporary decline in a population's fitness. In humans the term more often refers to disorders that may result from [[Incest|incest]] and [[Consanguinity|consanguinity]]. Breeders use inbreeding to establish new traits and to reveal harmful recessive alleles, which can then be removed through [[Selective breeding|selective breeding]]. In plant breeding, inbred lines are used to create [[Hybrid (biology)|hybrid]] lines that exploit heterosis. Avoiding inbreeding is the main selective reason for outcrossing.

[[Electric light]] that produces illumination by heating a filament until it glows. The [[Tungsten|tungsten]] filament is enclosed in a glass bulb that is evacuated or filled with inert gas to prevent oxidation. Bulbs work on either [[Alternating current|alternating]] or [[Direct current|direct current]], which made them widely used in homes, car headlamps and flashlights. Less than 5% of the energy they consume becomes visible light. A typical 120 V bulb produces 16 lumens per watt, compared with 60 for a compact fluorescent bulb and 100 for typical white LED lamps. Edison's version was the first practical implementation, although Joseph Swan's bulb was in daily use in London in 1881. Government efficiency standards have accelerated the shift from incandescent bulbs to LEDs.

Embodiment of a deity or spirit in earthly form, human or animal. The noun was originally coined for the union of divinity with humanity in [[Jesus]]. In Christianity, the Incarnation is the doctrine that God the Son, the second person of the [[Trinity]], became flesh, truly God and truly human. Mainstream [[Judaism]] has mostly rejected any incarnation of God since the time of [[Maimonides]], and Islamic theology categorically rejects it. [[Rastafari]] and the [[Druze]] faith hold beliefs in incarnation; the Druze considered the caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah an incarnation of God, a claim proclaimed in 1018. Hindu avatars, such as those of [[Vishnu]], are analogous but lack the permanent union of divine and human natures.

Aromatic material that releases fragrant smoke when burnt, or the aroma itself. Incense is used for aesthetic and religious reasons, [[Meditation|meditation]], aromatherapy, and as a deodorant or insect repellent. Direct-burning incense is lit by a flame and smolders, usually as a paste around a [[Bamboo|bamboo]] stick or extruded into a cone; indirect-burning incense needs a separate heat source. The word derives from Latin *incendere*, "to burn." One of the earliest known incense burners, from the A-Group culture (c. 3300–3000 BC), was found at Qustul in [[Nubia]]. In [[Ancient Egypt]] incense masked odors, repelled spirits and honored the gods. By about 2000 BC incense was used in ceremonies in China. Korean Buddhist monks brought it to Japan in the 6th century, and by the [[Heian period]] fine incense appreciation had become part of court culture.

2010 science fiction heist film written and directed by [[Christopher Nolan]]. [[Leonardo DiCaprio]] plays a thief who steals secrets by entering people's dreams and is offered a chance to clear his criminal record if he can implant an idea in a target's mind. The film was shot in six countries on a budget of US$160 million. It won four [[Academy Awards]], for cinematography, sound editing, sound mixing and visual effects, and received four further nominations. In 2025 the [[Library of Congress]] selected it for preservation in the National Film Registry.

Sexual activity between close relatives, such as siblings or a parent and child. The incest taboo is among the most widespread of cultural taboos, and most modern societies have laws against it. A common justification is avoiding [[Inbreeding|inbreeding]], since children of closely related parents face greater risk of congenital disorders. Anthropologists note, however, that prohibitions vary widely between cultures and do not necessarily maximize the avoidance of inbreeding. In [[Ancient Egypt]], royal families married within the family, such as brother and sister, to perpetuate the royal lineage. In [[Samoa]], a man could marry an older sister but not a younger one. Children of incestuous relationships have been regarded as illegitimate in some societies.

Unit of length in the British imperial and United States customary systems, equal to one-twelfth of a [[Foot (unit)|foot]]. The word derives from the Latin *uncia*, "one-twelfth." Since the international yard was adopted in the 1950s and 1960s, the inch has been defined as exactly 25.4 mm, or 2.54 cm. Its international standard symbol is *in*, though a double prime (″) is traditionally used. The inch is widely used for display screens such as [[Television|televisions]] and [[Computer monitor|computer monitors]] worldwide, and for vehicle wheel rims. Many metric countries, such as [[France]], [[Germany]] and [[Turkey]], supplement it with centimeters in advertisements and packaging. In the United Kingdom the inch remains a primary unit for road signs.

Flat supporting surface tilted at an angle, used as a ramp to raise or lower loads, and one of the six classical [[Simple machine|simple machines]] defined by [[Renaissance]] scientists. Moving a load up an inclined plane requires less force than lifting it, at the cost of a greater distance. Its mechanical advantage equals the ratio of the slope's length to its height. Because of [[Conservation of energy|conservation of energy]], the same work is needed, disregarding [[Friction|friction]]. The angle of repose is the steepest angle at which a load rests without sliding, equal to the arctangent of the coefficient of static friction. The [[Wedge|wedge]] and the screw are often considered derived from it. The Egyptian pyramids were built using inclined planes, and the stones of [[Stonehenge]] are believed to have been moved on them. Wheelchair ramps, loading ramps and roads climbing hills are common examples.
